input.quote: (h) This Agreement shall be governed by the laws of Nova Scotia and the laws of Canada applicable in Nova Scotia. All disputes under this Agreement shall be subject to the non-exclusive jurisdiction of the courts of Nova Scotia.
input.rationale: Section 20(h) is the only governing-law/venue provision (no arbitration clause appears anywhere; the sole reference to "arbitration fees" in the IP indemnity at p0090 is a costs reference only). The chosen law — Nova Scotia and the federal laws of Canada applicable there — is outside the playbook's accepted list (New York preferred; Delaware, California, or England and Wales as fallback), so on a literal parametric reading it fails the fallback. I am not treating this as a deviation to be redlined, however, because the clause runs in our favour and is nowhere near walk-away territory: Nova Scotia is our own home jurisdiction (Sparkling is at 19 Fielding Avenue, Dartmouth, NS per p0139), whereas the vendor is based in Saskatoon, Saskatchewan (p0138). The clause therefore gives us home-forum law and courts rather than the vendor's home jurisdiction, the venue grant is non-exclusive (preserving our ability to sue elsewhere, e.g. where the vendor's assets sit), and there is no mandatory arbitration and no foreign seat. Moving this to New York would strip our client of its home-court advantage and add cost and foreign-law risk, so the playbook's direction rule ("do not flag a clause that benefits our party") governs over the accepted-jurisdiction list here. Flagging for business confirmation only: if the deal team specifically wants a US-law contract for portfolio consistency, the minimal edit is to swap "Nova Scotia and the laws of Canada applicable in Nova Scotia" for New York law and the exclusive jurisdiction of the state and federal courts in New York County, leaving the rest of 20(h) intact. Absent that instruction, we recommend accepting 20(h) as drafted.
